problem: Contrastive VLN pre-training/fine-tuning only uses coarse-grained vision negatives (random shuffle, beam-search paths) while language negatives are fine-grained, so encoders align paths and instructions poorly on subtle path differences.
motivation: Hard negatives are known to improve contrastive embeddings, and Airbert showed fine-grained instruction negatives help. Choosing which frames of a path to replace to create effective fine-grained vision negatives is a hard search problem, so the paper uses Bayesian optimization.
key_idea: Use a TPE-based Bayesian optimizer in an adversarial min-max loop to choose which frames of a positive trajectory to replace, producing the hardest fine-grained vision negatives for contrastive path-instruction training.
insight: Replacing only a few BO-selected frames yields negatives whose embeddings the baseline (Lily) cannot separate; after training, fine-grained negatives are better separated (L2 mean 7.64 vs 4.72). Ablations on a data subset show BO masks beat a random selector (val_unseen SR 50.11 for random vs 53.14/56.45 for BO), delayed target updates help (~3% on val_unseen), and out-of-domain replacement frames beat in-domain ones. More BO iterations and two FGNs help unseen generalization.
method: Fine-grained negative generation: replace the frames marked by a binary mask M in the positive path with a replacement frame x_r (X_FG = v+·M̂ + x_r·M), keeping the positive instruction.
Inner maximization: a TPE Bayesian optimizer samples masks over trajectory frames for R iterations to maximize the target model's path-ranking contrastive loss, returning the best b masks S_M*.
Outer minimization: the online ViLBERT model is trained with the PR contrastive loss on the batch augmented with the b BO-selected fine-grained negatives plus the usual negatives.
Online/target models with delayed updates: the inner process uses a target copy of the online model, synced every J steps, for stable mask selection.
Replacement frame choice: out-of-domain frames (sampled from a different room) work better than in-domain ones.

Downstream adaptation: start from the Lily pre-trained model, fine-tune with MLM/MVM then PR with FGVLN, and use it as backbone of Recurrent VLN-BERT (imitation learning + A2C) for generative R2R and REVERIE.

setting.backbone: ViLBERT (initialized from Lily pre-training, fine-tuned with FGVLN); Recurrent VLN-BERT for the generative setting
setting.training_data: Lily pre-trained model (Airbnb/YouTube-based augmented data), then fine-tuned on R2R path-instruction pairs with BO-generated fine-grained negatives; generative R2R uses only original R2R data (no augmented data from EnvDrop)
setting.observation: egocentric panoramic RGB views along a path, plus the language instruction
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints (path ranking among candidates in the discriminative setting; step-wise viewpoint selection in the generative setting)
setting.privileged: none (the discriminative setting ranks pre-generated candidate paths)

results: FGVLN improves over Lily in discriminative R2R val-unseen (SR 67.69 vs 66.70, SPL 0.64 vs 0.62). In the generative setting it beats Rec(Airbert) on R2R val-unseen (SR 61 vs 59, SPL 55 vs 54) and on REVERIE (SR 28.71 vs 27.89, RGS 21.55 vs 18.23). Gains are modest.
limitations: Gains are small and NE is not always better (e.g., val-unseen NE 3.40 vs Lily 3.37; OSR below Airbert on REVERIE).
Ablations use an unspecified data subset and are run with a smaller batch size; the gain relies on extra compute for BO and two model copies.
Evaluated only on R2R and REVERIE in Matterport3D; no real-robot or continuous-environment tests.
